text: You get an array nums. The XOR total of a subset is the XOR of all its elements. The empty subset has total zero. Return the sum of the XOR totals over every subset.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — subsets with the same values but different positions count separately. So one, one has two subsets that are just one, and both add to the sum. Is that right? And the key thing: there are two to the n subsets, and I need one number from each. So I'll visit every subset once and add its XOR.
Yes. Each position is picked or not, on its own.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and twelve, and each value is between one and twenty.

OK. So at most two to the twelfth, which is four thousand ninety-six subsets. Enumerating all of them is fine. The biggest answer is small too. With twelve twenties I get forty thousand nine hundred sixty. If the OR of the values is thirty-one, it's sixty-three thousand four hundred eighty-eight. That fits in an int. Let me run through the example. One, three: the subsets are the empty one, which is zero; one; three; and one, three, which is one XOR three, two. The sum is zero plus one plus three plus two, six. Matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to build each subset as a real vector, then XOR it from scratch. That costs n per subset, so n times two to the n, plus copying. It works here, but it repeats a lot of work. This problem reminds me of the classic subsets backtracking pattern. Instead of storing the subset, I carry its XOR down the recursion as cur. Adding one element is just cur XOR nums at i. So each subset costs constant time.

Here's the plan. One: dfs takes a start index s and cur, the XOR so far. Two: add cur to the total as soon as I enter a call. Three: loop i from s, and recurse with i plus one and cur XOR nums at i. Here, I'm using cur to keep track of the subset's XOR; I never build the subset. One thing worth flagging — every node in the for-loop tree is a subset: the root is the empty set, and each child adds one element. So I add cur at every call, not only at the bottom. There's a trade-off here. The binary pick or skip tree is simpler to reason about, but it has two to the n plus one, minus one nodes, and only its leaves are subsets. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. total is an int reference, so every call adds into the same counter. When s equals n, the loop just doesn't run, and the call returns. One thing worth flagging — I pass cur XOR nums at i as a new value. I do not change cur itself. That keeps cur the same for every turn of the loop, so each sibling starts from the parent's subset. With cur XOR-equals nums at i instead, one, three gives five, not six, because the subset three starts from one. Also, I call it cur, not xor. In C++, xor is a reserved alternative token for the caret, so a parameter named xor is a compile error.
Works. Can you show the pick or skip version too?

Binary pick or skip — each element is either in or out. Let me walk through that. At depth i, I decide on nums at i. The left call picks it, the right call skips it. Only when i equals n is the subset complete, so only the leaves return a value. The inner nodes just add up their two children. No reference parameter needed.

Let's dry-run the code with five, one, six — expected twenty-eight. In the for-loop, the call that matters is number five: back in call two, cur is still five, so picking six gives five XOR six, three — not built on call three's four, because I never changed cur. Eight calls, eight subsets, total twenty-eight. The binary version gives the same twenty-eight in fifteen calls: eight leaves plus seven inner nodes, and the empty set is the last leaf instead of the root. Corner cases: three, four, five, six, seven, eight gives four hundred eighty. Recursing with s plus one, one, one, one gives nine instead of four. Mixing habits on one, one: adding only at the bottom of the for-loop gives one, adding at every node of the binary one gives three; expected two. A binary base case of n minus one turns a single one into zero.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is two to the n for both. Each call does constant work besides its children. The space complexity is linear, just the recursion depth. I never store a subset. In the worst-case scenario, n equals twelve, the constants differ. The for-loop makes exactly four thousand ninety-six calls, one per subset. The binary version makes eight thousand one hundred ninety-one calls, about twice as many, because the inner nodes are not subsets. Oh, one more thing — there's a linear formula. The answer is the OR of all the numbers, shifted left by n minus one. For each bit that appears in any number, exactly half of the subsets have that bit set in their XOR. It matched both versions on twenty thousand random arrays. I'd mention it as a follow-up, but backtracking is the pattern this problem is testing.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that in the for-loop every node is a subset, while in pick or skip only the leaves are, and you backed it with two to the n versus two to the n plus one, minus one calls. You explained why passing cur XOR nums at i instead of XOR-equals matters, with one, three giving five as proof. And you knew the OR shortcut as a follow-up. Good work.
